title: C++ Foundations
summary: The prerequisites. How to read a problem and derive the complexity you need before writing any code, the C++ you actually use under a one-second limit, and a proper treatment of OOP — classes as invariants, RAII, the rule of 0/3/5 — including an honest section on when *not* to use it in a contest.
metaTitle: C++ Foundations — approach, complexity, C++ and OOP
metaDescription: Problem-solving method, complexity analysis, competitive C++ and object-oriented design done properly.

title: Data Structures
summary: Every structure built from scratch as a class, against an interface, with its invariant stated up front. You will not reach for `std::stack` until you have written one. Each lesson follows the same shape: the problem it solves, the invariant, the implementation, the complexity table, the pitfalls.
metaTitle: Data Structures from scratch in C++
metaDescription: Dynamic arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, tries, graphs, DSU and range structures — each implemented as a class.

title: Algorithms
summary: The named algorithms and paradigms, with their complexity results: binary search and searching the answer space, graph traversal and shortest paths, topological order, dynamic programming in one and two dimensions, and greedy — including how to tell when a greedy choice is actually safe.
metaTitle: Algorithms — search, graphs, dynamic programming, greedy
metaDescription: Binary search, BFS and DFS, topological sort, shortest paths, 1-D and 2-D dynamic programming, and greedy with its proof obligations.

title: Competitive Approaches
summary: The recognition patterns — the shapes most interview problems reduce to. Two pointers, sliding windows, monotonic stacks, intervals and backtracking, taught as templates you learn to *spot*, because recognising the shape is the part that transfers. A solved problem you cannot classify teaches you almost nothing.
metaTitle: Competitive Approaches — the patterns that transfer
metaDescription: Two pointers, sliding window, monotonic stacks, intervals and backtracking as recognisable templates.
